rv.q: It’s been years—decades, really—since I last saw production numbers that were infused with the kind of rich, sustained creativity that Mr. Wheeldon gives us throughout “An American in Paris.”
This gorgeously danced — and just plain gorgeous — production pays loving tribute to the 1951 movie.
Gloriously inventive and balletic, it has an intriguing new book by Tony-nominee and Pulitzer Prize finalist Craig Lucas.
Just how extraordinary is unspooled all evening with exuberant, sweeping innovation, dark historical understanding and a big, smart heart.

Christopher Wheeldon's new musical An American in Paris is a gorgeous piece of work that succeeds in translating the dreamy romanticism of the 1951 film into a theatrical idiom that feels fresh and vital.
The touring production now at the Pantages through April 9 continues the magic of its 18-month Broadway run.

As directed by the choreographer Christopher Wheeldon and starring the dancers Robert Fairchild and Leanne Cope, An American in Paris is a fine and fanciful entertainment.

There's much gorgeous ballet to admire in choreographer Christopher Wheeldon's Broadway directorial debut, set against attractive, painterly backdrops by Bob Crowley, but the overall effect is of a dance concert with a semiserious musical squeezed into the cracks.
When those two are onstage, they make you believe in love — and the power of dance — all over again.
And while one is always grateful to hear them and to see artists at work with serious ideas, the result seems self-cancelling.

And the dancing in this new An American in Paris is sublime.
Regardless of the book, the music is glorious, the visuals are innovative and the performances are top-rate.
Dance is the only language really needed here.

This is a show that gets better and better as it goes along, building to a spectacular finale that will leave you breathless and wanting more.
That was the feeling at "An American in Paris," a colorful, charming, dazzlingly danced adaptation of the great 1951. Gene Kelly movie.

A dancer is a thing of beauty, and there is beaucoup beauty in director-choreographer Christopher Wheeldon's ravishing production of 'An American in Paris,' smartly but not slavishly adapted by Craig Lucas from the 1951 MGM movie.
Whether the cast is pirouetting and on toe or doing synchronized high kicks a la Busby Berkeley, the movements are elegant and energetic, witty and romantic.
As I say, you see this An American in Paris for the dancing.
At the same time, however, it feels like two shows.
Any one of Wheeldon's dances packs more content, smarts, and finesse than practically all the book scenes put together.
But when the dancing stops, it falls disappointingly flat.
Someone forgot to put the American in this “Paris.”
An American in Paris, one of the best musicals in recent memory.
This is not your typical Broadway musical — this is ballet set upon a Broadway stage, and it is simply remarkable.

This marvelous cast and ensemble cast all take a leading role in this exquisite production that will leave you standing on your feet, violently clapping, smiling from ear to ear with tears rolling down your cheeks.
In Paris is a thrilling addition to Broadway.
A visual, dance-driven Broadway story-telling creation that is gorgeous, enchanting, seamless and sophisticated.
The production achieves an integration of artistic and creative elements that is thoroughly realised.
An American in Paris is as smart and spirited as it is spectacular.
And so it is with An American in Paris; the fusion of the Broadway musical and ballet, set to the sublime music and lyrics of the Gershwin Brothers’ songbook, is an evening of pure enchantment.
And over half a century later, the wait was worth every minute.
Might we credit Christopher Wheeldon with presenting dance as one way to bring new light to the Broadway stage?
The final product feels to be a patchwork musical, indulging the audience with visual spectacles and beloved melodies at the expense of cohesive musical storytelling.

What this creative team has brought to a Broadway season currently awash in musical revivals is something innovative yet familiar, a gorgeous and moving tribute that emerges as a triumph for a new day.

While it’s impossible to dislike An American in Paris, it must be said that the show coasts on the familiarity of the songs and the stunning choreography which sometimes makes one wonder if it would’ve worked best as a full on ballet rather than a Broadway musical.
